title: Merge Operations to Turn Array Into a Palindrome
statement:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. In one operation you may choose two elements that sit next to each other and replace both of them with a single element equal to their sum, so the array becomes one element shorter.

Return the smallest number of operations after which `nums` is a palindrome, meaning it reads the same from left to right as from right to left. An array with one element is already a palindrome.
notes:
## Intuition

Whatever operations we apply, the final array is a split of `nums` into consecutive blocks, each replaced by its sum, and every merge removes exactly one element. Trying every split is exponential. Instead, look at the two ends: the first and last blocks of a palindrome must have equal sums. Because every value is positive, a block sum only grows as it absorbs neighbours, so the smaller end is the one that must grow, and it should take the very next element. Once both ends agree, matching them as early as possible never hurts the rest.

## Approach

1. Put `left` at the first index and `right` at the last; `leftSum` and `rightSum` hold the current end blocks.
2. While `left < right`:
   - If the sums are equal, the two ends match: step both pointers inward and start fresh blocks.
   - If `leftSum` is smaller, merge the next element into the left block and count one operation.
   - Otherwise merge the previous element into the right block and count one operation.
3. Return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [4,3,2,1,2,3,1]`. Start with `leftSum = 4`, `rightSum = 1`. Since `4 > 1`, the right block absorbs `3` to become `4` (`operations = 1`). The ends match, so the pointers move to `3` and `2`. Now `3 > 2`, so the right block absorbs `1` to become `3` (`operations = 2`). They match again and `left` meets `right` at the middle `2`. The array is now `[4,3,2,3,4]` and the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each step moves one pointer inward.
- Space: O(1): only two indices and two sums.

## Pitfalls

- Merge into the smaller side only; growing the larger side can never make them equal.
- After matching, reload both sums from the new positions instead of carrying the old totals.
- Sums reach about 10^11, which overflows a 32-bit integer in Java or C; use a 64-bit type there.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left`, `right` | indices of the last element in the current left and right blocks |
| `leftSum`, `rightSum` | sums of the current left and right blocks |
| `operations` | merges performed so far |

narration.2: The left pointer starts at the first element.
narration.3: The right pointer starts at the last element.
narration.4: The current left block holds just its first element.
narration.5: The current right block holds just its last element.
narration.8: Keep working while there are still two separate ends to match.
narration.9: Equal block sums mean the two ends already mirror each other.
narration.10: Move the left pointer inward past the matched block.
narration.11: Move the right pointer inward past the matched block.
narration.12: Start a new left block at the new left position.
narration.13: Start a new right block at the new right position.
narration.14: The left block is smaller, so it must grow to have any chance of matching.
narration.15: Step left onto the next element.
narration.16: Merge that element into the left block.
narration.18: Otherwise the right block is smaller, so it must grow instead.
narration.19: Step right onto the previous element.
narration.20: Merge the previous element into the right block.
narration.24: The pointers met, so the array is a palindrome; return the merges used.
